hints: Start by picturing the blue ion $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ with six water ligands arranged octahedrally around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.
Think about what $\text{OH}^-$ ions do to aqua complexes of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, does a water ligand get swapped or does an insoluble hydroxide form?
Recall the characteristic colour and state of copper(II) hydroxide formed from aqueous $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.
For concentrated $\text{HCl}$, consider the very high concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands competing with water for the copper centre.
Remember the name given when one ligand directly replaces another in the coordination sphere without change in oxidation state.
Recall the characteristic colour of the tetrachlorocuprate(II) complex $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ formed in excess concentrated chloride.
walkthrough:
See what hydroxide does to the aqua complex**
Picture $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ in solution. When you add $\text{OH}^-$, the hydroxide is a base and removes protons from coordinated water at first, but with copper the overall result is that the aqua complex is destroyed and neutral copper(II) hydroxide comes out of solution. That is why we call it precipitation, not ligand exchange. The balanced ionic equation keeps copper balanced and shows the six waters released:
$$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Link the precipitate to its appearance**
Copper(II) hydroxide is very distinctive. It is a pale blue solid that appears as a blue precipitate in the colourless solution. Remember to give both colour and state, blue on its own is not enough for the mark.

See what excess chloride does to the aqua complex**
Now imagine flooding that same blue solution with concentrated $\text{HCl}$. There is a huge excess of $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. These chloride ligands compete for the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ centre and completely replace all six water molecules. The coordination number changes from 6 to 4 and a new complex forms:
$$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{CuCl}_4^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Check it: Cu is 1 to 1, Cl is 4 to 4, H and O balance as $6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and charge balances as $2+ + 4(-1) = 2-$ on both sides.

Name the reaction type and appearance correctly**
Because $\text{Cl}^-$ directly swaps for $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the coordination sphere with no change in oxidation number of copper, this is ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution, displacement or replacement. The product $\text{CuCl}_4^{2-}$ stays dissolved, so you see a yellow solution, very different from the starting blue solution and from a blue precipitate.

Final answer: Reaction with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$:
$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
type: precipitation
blue precipitate

Reaction with concentrated $\text{HCl}$:
$[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{CuCl}_4^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
type: ligand exchange / substitution / displacement
 yellow solution

hints: Use $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$ to find moles of $\text{Ag}^+$ used in the $25.00 \text{ cm}^3$ titre, then scale up to the full $100.0 \text{ cm}^3$ flask.
Use the 1:1 equation $\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl}$ to get moles of $\text{Cl}^-$, convert to mass of $\text{Cl}$, then subtract from $0.303 \text{ g}$ to leave mass of S.
Convert mass of S to moles using $32.1$ and compare moles of S with moles of $\text{Cl}$ in the original sample to get the simplest whole number ratio.
walkthrough:
Find moles of chloride from the titre**
The titration tells you how much $\text{Cl}^-$ was in the $25.00 \text{ cm}^3$ portion. First convert volume to $\text{dm}^3$:
$$V = \frac{22.40}{1000} = 0.02240 \text{ dm}^3$$
$$n(\text{Ag}^+) = c \times V = 0.0500 \times 0.02240 = 1.12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
Because $$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(\text{s})$$ is 1:1, this is also $1.12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cl}^-$ in $25.00 \text{ cm}^3$. The bulk solution is $100.0 \text{ cm}^3$, which is four times larger, so multiply by 4:
$$n(\text{Cl}^- \text{ in } 100.0 \text{ cm}^3) = 1.12 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 = 4.48 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Split the 0.303 g into Cl mass and S mass**
Convert those chloride moles to mass using $A_r(\text{Cl}) = 35.5$:
$$m(\text{Cl}) = 4.48 \times 10^{-3} \times 35.5 = 0.159 \text{ g}$$
This $0.159 \text{ g}$ of Cl came from the original $0.303 \text{ g}$ of sulfur chloride, so the rest must be sulfur:
$$m(\text{S}) = 0.303 - 0.159 = 0.144 \text{ g}$$

Turn masses into a mole ratio**
Now convert sulfur mass to moles with $A_r(\text{S}) = 32.1$:
$$n(\text{S}) = \frac{0.144}{32.1} = 4.49 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
Compare:
$$n(\text{S}) : n(\text{Cl}) = 4.49 \times 10^{-3} : 4.48 \times 10^{-3} \approx 1:1$$
So the simplest ratio is one S to one Cl, giving empirical formula $\text{SCl}$.

Final answer: In $25.00 \text{ cm}^3$: $n(\text{Ag}^+) = 0.0500 \times 0.02240 = 1.12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
In $100.0 \text{ cm}^3$: $n(\text{Ag}^+) = 1.12 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 = 4.48 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol} = n(\text{Cl}^-)$
$m(\text{Cl}) = 4.48 \times 10^{-3} \times 35.5 = 0.159 \text{ g}$
$m(\text{S}) = 0.303 - 0.159 = 0.144 \text{ g}$
$n(\text{S}) = 0.144 / 32.1 = 4.49 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$n(\text{S}) : n(\text{Cl}) = 1:1$, empirical formula = $\text{SCl}$
